raw_case_text:
A 38-year-old male presented with an episode of giddiness and uneasiness that lasted for 2 days. There was no history of dyspnea or palpitation. He did not have any comorbid illness. Clinical examination revealed bitemporal hemianopia and biochemical evaluation showed hyponatremia, hypocortisolism, and hypothyroidism, with elevated follicle-stimulating hormone, luteinizing hormone, and testosterone []. Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) brain revealed a sellar-supra-sellar mass [Figure 1]. After hormone supplementation and correction of electrolytes, he underwent gross total excision of the tumor through endonasal trans-sphenoidal route. During the perioperative period, he was given hydrocortisone infusion at 4 mg/h and during the immediate postoperative period, he was given hydrocortisone 50 mg intravenously 8th hourly. The intraoperative and immediate postoperative period was uneventful, and he was discharged on glucocorticoid (oral hydrocortisone 10 mg/m2 /day) and thyroxine replacement. Histopathology and immunohistochemistry showed a gonadotropin secreting pituitary adenoma. The dura and bone was free of tumor, and the sphenoid sinus mucosa was normal.
Three weeks later, he presented with intermittent fever and cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) rhinorrhea of 5 days duration. On examination, he had terminal neck rigidity. CSF studies were suggestive of pyogenic meningitis, CSF culture showed Enterobacter species, and he was started on appropriate antibiotics. The computed tomography (CT) scan showed pneumocephalus. Endoscopic repair of the defect was done after the infection was apparently controlled, and CSF was diverted through an external lumbar drain, to aid healing. Despite the repair, CSF rhinorrhea persisted, and CT scan showed the progression of pneumocephalus. Repeat CSF culture after a week grew Staphylococcus and he was started on intravenous Vancomycin and Meropenem with intrathecal Vancomycin. His preoperative total leukocyte count was 8700 mm3 with neutrophils 71%, lymphocytes 22%, monocytes 5%, and eosinophils 2%. At present admission, his total leukocyte count was 15,800 with neutrophils 82%, lymphocytes 14%, and monocytes 4%. His serum albumin and globulin were 4.5 g/dl and 3.5 g/dl, respectively. Serology for HIV was negative. The serial CSF reports of the patient are given in the . Throughout the course, he was on therapy with injectable hydrocortisone 50 mg every 8th hourly and thyroxine 100 mug, and required subcutaneous desmopressin intermittently for diabetes insipidus. After 3 weeks of hospital stay, he suddenly became unresponsive and CT scan showed a subarachnoid hemorrhage with intraventricular extension [Figure 2]. The patient expired a day later, despite the external ventricular drainage.
The cause of death was speculated to be due to rupture of an intracranial aneurysm. This may have been an association with pituitary macroadenoma (although it is seen often with functioning pituitary macroadenoma), or due to the weakening of vessel wall due to inflammatory exudates. The third possibility could be an inadvertent intraoperative injury such as snapping of a perforator from a distal vessel, resulting in pseudoaneurysm formation. To confirm the cause of death, a limited brain autopsy was performed, which revealed extensive subarachnoid hemorrhage and aneurysmal dilatation and thrombosis of the basilar artery (BA) [Figure 3]. There were multiple hemorrhagic infarcts in the midbrain and pons. Histopathology of the BA revealed the loss of internal elastic lamina and septate hyphae with an acute angle branching on Grocott's methenamine silver stain, conforming to the morphology of Aspergillus [Figure 4a-d].

subjective.chief_complaint: A 38-year-old male presented initially with a 2-day history of giddiness and uneasiness due to a pituitary macroadenoma, and returned 3 weeks after endonasal transsphenoidal resection with a 5-day history of intermittent fever and cerebrospinal fluid rhinorrhea.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: The patient initially presented with 2 days of giddiness and bitemporal hemianopia, underwent uneventful endonasal transsphenoidal gross total excision of a gonadotropin-secreting pituitary macroadenoma under perioperative hydrocortisone coverage, and was discharged on oral hydrocortisone and thyroxine replacement. Three weeks postoperatively, he re-presented with 5 days of intermittent fever and CSF rhinorrhea. Despite antibiotic therapy for Enterobacter and subsequent Staphylococcus meningitis, endoscopic skull base defect repair, and lumbar CSF drainage, CSF rhinorrhea and pneumocephalus persisted, and 3 weeks into readmission he suddenly became unresponsive.
subjective.past_medical_history: Gonadotropin-secreting pituitary macroadenoma with secondary hypocortisolism and hypothyroidism, status post endonasal transsphenoidal resection 3 weeks prior; postoperative diabetes insipidus managed with intermittent subcutaneous desmopressin.
subjective.review_of_systems: Initial presentation: giddiness, uneasiness, visual field loss (negative for dyspnea or palpitations). Readmission: intermittent fever, persistent CSF rhinorrhea, neck stiffness, and subsequent sudden coma.

objective.physical_examination: Initial exam showed bitemporal hemianopia. On readmission 3 weeks postoperatively, exam revealed terminal neck rigidity and CSF rhinorrhea. Three weeks into readmission, he became acutely unresponsive/comatose.
objective.routine_investigations: Baseline pre-op labs showed hyponatremia, hypocortisolism, hypothyroidism, elevated FSH, LH, and testosterone, and WBC 8,700/mm3. Readmission labs showed leukocytosis (WBC 15,800/mm3 with 82% neutrophils, 14% lymphocytes, 4% monocytes), albumin 4.5 g/dL, globulin 3.5 g/dL, and negative HIV serology. Initial readmission CSF analysis showed pyogenic meningitis with culture growing Enterobacter species; repeat CSF culture 1 week after endoscopic repair grew Staphylococcus species.
objective.advanced_workup: Initial brain MRI showed a sellar-suprasellar pituitary mass, confirmed histologically as a gonadotropin-secreting pituitary adenoma with normal sphenoid mucosa. Readmission head CTs demonstrated progressive pneumocephalus, and emergent head CT following sudden unresponsiveness at week 3 of readmission showed massive basal subarachnoid hemorrhage with intraventricular extension. Limited postmortem brain autopsy revealed extensive subarachnoid hemorrhage, multiple midbrain and pontine hemorrhagic infarcts, and aneurysmal dilatation and thrombosis of the basilar artery; histopathology of the basilar artery wall (Grocott methenamine silver stain) demonstrated loss of the internal elastic lamina and invasion by acute-angle branching septate hyphae of Aspergillus.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation: Fatal ruptured Aspergillus mycotic aneurysm of the basilar artery causing massive subarachnoid and intraventricular hemorrhage and brainstem infarction complicating post-transsphenoidal CSF leak and bacterial meningitis (Enterobacter and Staphylococcus), definitively confirmed at autopsy by Grocott methenamine silver histopathology of the basilar artery wall demonstrating acute-angle branching septate Aspergillus hyphae. Despite endoscopic CSF leak repair, external lumbar drainage, IV/intrathecal vancomycin and meropenem, stress-dose hydrocortisone, and emergent external ventricular drainage after aneurysmal rupture, the patient died the following day.
